# Data Report

This data report documents all datasets used in the project in order to ensure transparency, traceability and reproducibility. Since the project combines multiple statistical sources to visualise different dimensions of generational differences in Switzerland, particular attention is paid to the origin, structure, quality and transformation of the data.

The report distinguishes between raw data and processed data. Raw data refers to the original files as obtained from public statistical sources. Processed data refers to cleaned, harmonised and transformed datasets that are used directly in the Streamlit application. This distinction is important because the original data sources often differ in structure, naming conventions, temporal coverage and level of aggregation.

The purpose of this documentation is not only to describe the data technically, but also to make methodological decisions explicit. This includes the harmonisation of age groups, the selection of relevant indicators, the treatment of missing values and the limitations resulting from aggregated public data.

## Raw Data

The raw datasets are documented according to the three main dimensions of the project: **Who decides?**, **Who pays?**, and **Who owns?**. This thematic structure follows the logic of the final visualisation and makes it transparent which data sources are used for each analytical perspective.

### Details Raw Data: Who Decides – Political Participation and Voting Behaviour

The raw data for the dimension **"Who decides?"** consists of three post-election survey datasets from the Swiss Electoral Study (SELECTS), covering the federal elections of 2015, 2019 and 2023. The surveys are conducted by FORS (Swiss Centre of Expertise in the Social Sciences) at the Université de Lausanne and are accessible through the FORS data archive under a standard research data licence for non-commercial academic use. The datasets do not contain individually identifiable data and are considered reliable reference data for Swiss electoral behaviour research.

The three files were accessed as follows:

- `data/whodecide/raw/726_Selects2015_PES_Data_v1.03.dta` — SELECTS 2015 raw data in Stata format
- `data/whodecide/processed/selects_2015_clean.csv` — Preprocessed 2015 data
- `data/whodecide/processed/selects_2019_clean.csv` — Preprocessed 2019 data
- `data/whodecide/processed/selects_2023_clean.csv` — Preprocessed 2023 data

The raw files are not directly suitable for visualisation because variable names and coding conventions differ across survey waves. In particular, the left–right self-placement variable uses a 7-point scale in 2015 (`f12900main7`), whereas 2019 and 2023 use a recoded 5-point scale (`f12900rec`, values 10/20/30/40/50). Preprocessing was therefore required to harmonise all three waves into a consistent analytical structure and assign generation labels.

#### Data Catalogue

The data catalogue below describes the harmonised schema produced by the preprocessing pipeline (`who_decides_section.py`). All three processed CSV files share this schema after loading and standardisation. The original SELECTS variable names are retained where possible to ensure traceability back to the source codebooks.

: Data catalogue for the harmonised "Who decides?" datasets. {#tbl-whodecides-data-catalogue}

| Column index | Column name | Datatype | Values / validation rules | Short description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `birthyear` | integer | Approximately 1920–2005, depending on survey wave | Birth year of the respondent. Used to derive generation assignment. |
| 2 | `generation` | string / categorical | `Silent Generation`, `Babyboomers`, `Generation X`, `Millennials / Gen Y`, `Generation Z` | Generation label derived from birth year using fixed cut-off points. Cut-offs: Silent ≤ 1945, Boomers ≤ 1964, Gen X ≤ 1980, Millennials ≤ 1996, Gen Z > 1996. |
| 3 | `voted` | integer | 0 = did not vote, 1 = voted | Binary indicator of self-reported voter turnout. Derived from `f11100rec` (2019/2023) or `f11100r` (2015 CSV variant). Only non-negative values are retained; invalid codes are excluded. |
| 4 | `political_interest` | float | 1–4 scale (1 = not at all interested, 4 = very interested); codes −99, −98, 9 treated as missing | Self-reported level of interest in politics. Derived from `f10100`. |
| 5 | `trust_avg` | float | Mean of three trust items, each on a scale approximately 1–10; codes −99, −98 treated as missing | Average institutional trust score across three items: trust in the federal government (`f11301`), trust in parliament (`f11302`), and satisfaction with democracy (`f11305`). |
| 6 | `demo_satisfaction` | integer | 0 = not satisfied, 1 = satisfied; codes −99, −98, 8, 9 treated as missing | Binary indicator of democratic satisfaction. Derived from `f12010` (original values: 1 → satisfied, 2 → not satisfied). |
| 7 | `lr_scale` | float | 1.0–5.0 continuous scale (1 = far left, 5 = far right); codes −99, −98 treated as missing | Left–right self-placement. In 2015: derived from `f12900main7` (7-point scale mapped to 1–5 via fixed mapping). In 2019/2023: derived from `f12900rec` (values 10/20/30/40/50 divided by 10). |

The three processed CSVs do not contain a common `survey_year` column; the year dimension is introduced at load time by the pipeline, which reads each file separately and keys the resulting DataFrames by election year (2015, 2019, 2023).

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The exploratory analysis showed that the SELECTS data is well suited for a generational comparison of political participation across three election cycles, but requires careful handling of several methodological issues.

**Sample sizes and generation coverage.** The three survey waves have the following approximate sample sizes: SELECTS 2015 (N ≈ 5 337), SELECTS 2019 (N ≈ 6 664) and SELECTS 2023 (N ≈ 5 033). After filtering for valid turnout responses and assigning generation labels, the effective analytical sample per wave is somewhat smaller. The Silent Generation cohort is structurally small in recent waves due to demographic attrition, which means that point estimates for this generation should be interpreted with caution in 2019 and 2023. Generation Z respondents are also comparatively few because many members of this cohort were below the voting age of 18 in earlier survey waves.

**Self-reported turnout bias.** Voter turnout in the SELECTS surveys is self-reported. It is well established in electoral survey research that self-reported turnout systematically overestimates actual turnout due to social desirability bias: respondents are more likely to report having voted than they actually did. The parliament chart (chart 1) therefore does not show individual turnout rates but rather the *compositional share* of self-reported voters by generation — this framing reduces the impact of overreporting bias while preserving the key finding that older generations dominate the active electorate.

**Variable coding differences across waves.** As described above, the left–right self-placement variable differs structurally between 2015 (7-point scale) and 2019/2023 (5-point recoded scale). The mapping applied in the preprocessing pipeline (`{1:1.0, 2:1.5, 3:2.5, 4:3.0, 5:3.5, 6:4.5, 7:5.0}`) is a reasonable approximation but introduces some uncertainty in cross-wave comparisons. Trend interpretations for the left–right chart should therefore be treated with caution, particularly for the 2015–2019 transition.

**Missing value treatment.** SELECTS uses standardised missing value codes (−99 = not answered, −98 = does not apply, 9 or 8 = refused or invalid). All such codes are recoded to `NaN` during preprocessing. Aggregations at generation level use only non-missing observations. Where missingness rates are high for a particular generation and year, this is reflected in gaps in the visualisation rather than imputed values.

**Data quality assessment.** Overall, the data quality is sufficient for the intended visualisation purpose. The three survey waves are methodologically consistent, cover the required variables, and are the standard reference source for Swiss electoral behaviour research. The main limitations — self-report bias, varying sample sizes for edge-case generations, and the left–right coding change — are documented here and should be acknowledged when interpreting trends in the "Who decides?" section of the dashboard.


### Details Raw Data: Home / Demographics – Demographic Balance of Switzerland

The raw data for the **Home page** demographic visualisations (generational area chart and population pyramid) consists of a single dataset from the Swiss Federal Statistical Office (BFS).

**Source:** Bundesamt für Statistik (BFS). (2024). *Demografische Bilanz der Schweiz*. Neuchâtel: BFS. Retrieved from https://www.bfs.admin.ch

**Storage location:** `data/demografischeBilanz.csv`

The file contains Swiss population data by birth year and calendar year, covering 1981–2024. It is the primary source for assigning population counts to the five generational cohorts (Silent Generation, Babyboomers, Generation X, Millennials / Gen Y, Generation Z) as defined in `app_config.py`. The data is loaded at application startup by `demographic_section.py` via `load_demographic_data()`. Generation labels are derived dynamically from birth year using fixed cut-off points. The dataset does not contain individual-level data and is published as an aggregated official statistic. No missing values are present. The temporal coverage (1981–2024) is sufficient to show the full demographic shift from a Boomer-dominant to a more balanced generational distribution.

### Details Raw Data: Who Pays - Financial Contributions and Public Transfers

The raw data for the analytical dimension **“Who pays?”** consists of multiple datasets that are combined in a dedicated data acquisition pipeline. This dimension focuses on financial contributions, mandatory payments and age-related public transfers in Switzerland. The aim is to analyse how financial burdens and benefits differ between generations and how these patterns change over time.

The data acquisition script `01_data_acquisition/load_whopays_final.py` combines three separate source areas: mandatory health insurance data (OKP), AHV income data and AHV expenditure data. In addition, population data from the Swiss Federal Statistical Office is used as an auxiliary dataset to derive age- and cohort-related indicators. The script explicitly keeps the original raw files unchanged and writes the cleaned and harmonised outputs to `data/whopays/processed_whopays/`.

The mandatory health insurance data is stored in `data/whopays/raw_whopays/`. The raw files consist of annual Excel files and ZIP archives from the Swiss health insurance statistics. The extraction logic uses different file groups because the structure of the original files changes over time. For the configured OKP extraction, the script distinguishes between files for 2006–2010, 2011–2021 and 2022–2024. Relevant statistical tables are extracted from the original Excel workbooks, including indicators such as premiums, premium reductions, cost sharing, net benefits and gross benefits.

The AHV-related raw data is stored in the same raw data directory. The file `ahv_einnahmen_zhaw.xlsx` is used for AHV income-related information, while `px-x-1305000000_103_20260416-235225.xlsx` is used for AHV expenditure-related information. These datasets are processed together with population data in order to derive indicators by age, birth year and generation.

The population data is loaded from `data/raw/px-x-0102020000_103_20260424-164251.xlsx`. It is used as an auxiliary dataset rather than as a main thematic dataset. The pipeline reads age-specific population data by year and calculates an average population value based on the population at the beginning and end of the year. This average population is then used as a weighting basis for age-related transformations.

The raw files are not directly suitable for visualisation because they differ in file format, internal sheet structure, naming conventions and temporal coverage. Some files are provided as Excel workbooks, while others are compressed ZIP archives containing multiple statistical tables. Therefore, the raw data requires substantial preprocessing before it can be used in the Streamlit application. The main preprocessing steps include selecting relevant sheets, extracting age-group rows, parsing age labels, cleaning numeric values, harmonising variable names and mapping birth years to generations.

From a data governance perspective, the datasets used in this dimension are aggregated statistical datasets. They do not contain individual-level personal data and can therefore be treated as public or project-relevant aggregated data. However, the resulting indicators should be interpreted carefully because the underlying sources differ in structure, aggregation level and statistical definition. The processed outputs are therefore best understood as analytical approximations of generational financial burden rather than exact individual-level accounting.

#### Data Catalogue

The raw data for the **“Who pays?”** dimension originates from heterogeneous Excel files, ZIP archives and official statistical exports. Since the original files differ in structure, sheet names, age-group definitions and temporal coverage, the data catalogue below describes the harmonised schema produced by the data acquisition pipeline. This schema is used as the basis for the exploratory analysis and the Streamlit visualisation.

The processed datasets for this dimension are stored in `data/whopays/processed_whopays/`.

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The exploratory analysis showed that the data for the **“Who pays?”** dimension is suitable for a high-level visualisation of generational financial burden, but only after substantial preprocessing and with several methodological limitations.

The main quality issue is structural heterogeneity. The OKP/KVSTAT data is provided as a series of annual Excel files and ZIP archives whose internal structure changes over time. Sheet names, available tables and column positions are not fully consistent across years. For this reason, the data acquisition script uses separate extraction logic for different file groups and explicitly selects the relevant statistical tables. The main OKP tables used in the project include premium-related indicators, premium reductions, cost sharing, net benefits and gross benefits by age group.

A second important issue is the harmonisation of age groups. The original OKP and AHV datasets are often provided in age cohorts rather than single-year ages. To make the data comparable across generations, these cohort-level values are disaggregated to single ages using population weights. The population data provides age-specific population counts by year. The pipeline calculates an average population value from the population at the beginning and end of the year and uses this as the weighting basis. This method improves comparability but remains an approximation: values within an age group are distributed proportionally to population size, not observed directly at individual age level.

For the OKP data, the relevant variables include premiums, premium reductions, cost sharing, net benefits and gross benefits. These variables should not be interpreted as identical forms of financial burden. For example, a net health insurance burden would conceptually require combining several components, such as premiums, premium reductions and cost sharing. Therefore, visualisations based only on premiums show the payment side of the system, but not necessarily the full net burden after subsidies.

The AHV income data has an important limitation: it only covers employees. Self-employed persons and non-employed persons are not included in the age-specific AHV income dataset. This means that the calculated number of contributors and contribution sums underestimate the full AHV contribution base. The macro-level dataset `ahv_makro.csv` is therefore used as a plausibility check against official aggregate contribution totals. In the exploratory analysis, the deviation between the employee-based dataset and the macro-level control values was consistent and plausible. This supports the use of the data for trend analysis, while still requiring clear documentation of the missing contributor groups.

The AHV expenditure data has a different structure. It covers pension recipients and therefore mainly concerns persons aged 65 and older. Younger age groups do not appear in the old-age pension data because they do not receive regular AHV old-age pensions. This is not a data error, but a structural characteristic of the Swiss old-age pension system. The variable `renten_mittelwert_chf` represents a monthly pension value, not an annual value, and must therefore not be divided by twelve during analysis.

The comparison between AHV contributions and AHV benefits is analytically meaningful, but must be interpreted carefully. Contribution values describe what an individual contributor or contributor group pays into the system, while pension values describe what a pension recipient receives. This reflects the logic of a pay-as-you-go pension system. The ratio between contributors and pension recipients is therefore an important contextual indicator. In the available data, the number of contributors per pension recipient decreased from approximately 3.49 in 2012 to approximately 3.22 in 2024. Since the contributor count only includes employees, the absolute level of this ratio is conservative, but the downward trend remains informative.

Several generation-specific values require caution. Very young generations, especially Generation Alpha, should not be interpreted as economically meaningful AHV contributors, because children do not usually pay AHV contributions. Similarly, values for the Silent Generation on the contribution side represent only a very small remaining employed group. For this reason, the AHV contribution visualisation should focus primarily on economically active generations where the interpretation is meaningful.

Overall, the data quality is sufficient for the intended visualisation goal: to show broad generational patterns in mandatory payments, social insurance contributions and public transfers. However, the results should be interpreted as aggregated and methodologically harmonised indicators, not as exact individual-level accounting. The main limitations are the use of population-weighted disaggregation, differences in temporal coverage, changes in raw file structure, missing contributor groups in the AHV income data and the different interpretation of payment-side and benefit-side indicators.

### Details Raw Dataset: Who Owns – Housing Tenure and Living Space

The raw data for the analytical dimension **"Who owns?"** consists of multiple datasets that document housing tenure status, living space per person and cantonal homeownership rates across Switzerland. This dimension focuses on how residential property ownership and available housing resources are distributed across age groups and generations. The aim is to analyse whether different generations own or rent their homes, how much living space they have available, and how these patterns relate to structural barriers in the Swiss housing market.

The data acquisition script `01_data_acquisition/load_sources.py` loads three separate source areas: occupancy type data, living space data, and cantonal homeownership rate data. The script explicitly retains the original raw files unchanged and writes the cleaned outputs to `data/whoOwns/processed/`.

The primary raw file is `data/whoOwns/raw/bfs_bewohnertyp_groesse.xlsx`. This Excel workbook is provided by the Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO) and contains two distinct types of statistical tables embedded in separate sheets. The first type is stored in sheets prefixed with `SE` (Strukturerhebung, i.e. the Federal Structural Survey). These sheets contain occupancy type data by single age year for the years 2019 to 2024. For each age and year, the data provides the absolute number of persons by occupancy type — owner, renter or cooperative member, other situation — along with share percentages and associated confidence intervals. The second type is stored in sheets prefixed with `GWS-STATPOP`. These sheets contain the average living space in square metres per person by single age year, also for the years 2019 to 2024. This data is derived from the Federal Register of Buildings and Dwellings (GWS) linked with the Federal Population Register (STATPOP) and covers the entire permanently resident population rather than relying on survey sampling alone.

The second raw source is `data/whoOwns/raw/wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026.csv`. This is a BFS statistical export providing homeownership rates by Swiss canton and year, using semicolons as delimiters. Geographic units are identified using BFS geographic codes (e.g. `CH040` for Uri, `CH010` for Zurich). An accompanying metadata file, `data/whoOwns/raw/metadaten_wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026.ods`, provides a mapping between BFS geographic codes and canton names in four languages (German, French, Italian, English). During data acquisition, this metadata is joined onto the cantonal data to enrich the geographic identifiers with human-readable labels.

A fourth file, `data/whoOwns/raw/statistik_vermoegen_2022.xlsx`, is present in the raw data directory but is not integrated into the current visualisation pipeline. It contains aggregate wealth statistics from 2022 and was considered during the initial data exploration phase but was ultimately not used because its level of aggregation was not compatible with the age- and generation-based analysis structure of the project.

The raw files are not directly suitable for visualisation because they differ in file format, internal sheet structure and naming conventions. In the `bfs_bewohnertyp_groesse.xlsx` workbook, the year must be inferred from the sheet name because the sheets do not contain a dedicated year column. Column names in the raw sheets contain multi-line headers with special characters and encoding artifacts that require cleaning. The cantonal ownership data uses semicolons as delimiters rather than commas, and the geographic codes require a separate join to obtain readable canton names. The main preprocessing steps therefore include identifying and loading the relevant sheets per data type, inferring the reference year from the sheet name, parsing and cleaning age and occupancy type labels, converting numeric columns from string to float, standardising column names to lowercase with whitespace stripped, and filtering out total rows and non-numeric placeholders. The script distinguishes between `bewohnertyp` and `wohnflaeche` sheet types through a name-matching heuristic that checks for keywords in the sheet name.

From a data governance perspective, all datasets used in this dimension are aggregated statistical datasets published by the Swiss Federal Statistical Office (FSO). They are derived from official administrative registers and the annual Federal Structural Survey (Strukturerhebung), and are accessible for research and educational purposes under FSO data usage conditions. The datasets do not contain individual-level personal data and can therefore be treated as public, aggregate statistical information. However, results must be interpreted with the understanding that the Structural Survey covers only persons aged 15 and older who are part of the permanent resident population and live in private households. Persons residing in collective households — such as care homes, assisted living facilities or other institutional accommodation — are excluded from the survey by design. This exclusion disproportionately affects the oldest age groups, particularly the Silent Generation, because a significant share of very old persons live in care homes. As a consequence, occupancy and living space values for the Silent Generation are likely biased toward owner-occupied large dwellings, since those who remain in private households tend to live in the homes they have owned for decades. This limitation is documented explicitly in the visualisation and must be kept in mind when comparing the Silent Generation with younger generations.

#### Data Catalogue

The raw data for the **"Who owns?"** dimension originates from a combined FSO Excel workbook and a supplementary CSV export. Since the original file uses different sheet prefixes to separate occupancy type and living space data, and since both the year and the data type must be inferred from the sheet name during loading, the data catalogue below describes the harmonised schemas of the three processed output files produced by the data acquisition pipeline.

The processed datasets for this dimension are stored in `data/whoOwns/processed/`.

No single master table was created before the exploratory analysis because the occupancy type and living space data differ in structure, units, age coverage and statistical derivation method. The cantonal homeownership file has a different unit of analysis (canton rather than individual age) and is therefore kept separate. Keeping the analytical files separate reduces unnecessary complexity and makes the methodological origin of each indicator transparent.

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The exploratory analysis showed that the data for the **"Who owns?"** dimension is well-suited for a high-level visualisation of generational housing patterns, but with several structural characteristics and limitations that must be considered.

The occupancy type dataset (`bfs_bewohnertyp_20260414_clean.csv`) has 2,040 rows covering ages 15 to approximately 100 across six years (2019–2024) and four occupancy type categories, including a `Total` row per age. The `Total` rows are filtered out in the Streamlit application to avoid double-counting when aggregating by generation. The three substantive occupancy types are `Eigentümer` (owner), `Mieter oder Genossenschafter` (renter or cooperative member) and `Andere Situation` (other situation, e.g. dwelling provided free of charge by a relative or employer). The `Andere Situation` category represents a consistently small share across all age groups and is excluded from the visualisation because it does not contribute meaningfully to the generational comparison.

The confidence intervals in the occupancy data are provided per cell and reflect the sampling uncertainty of the Federal Structural Survey. They tend to be larger at the extremes of the age distribution — for very young adults (15–19) and very old persons (above 80) — because the sample sizes are smaller in those groups. The `datenqualität` column contains a data quality flag (typically `*`) for cells where the FSO considers the estimate to have limited reliability. In the current visualisation, these flagged cells are used as-is, but the affected age groups fall in the margins of the generation distribution where the interpretation is already treated with caution.

The living space dataset (`bfs_wohnflaeche_20260414_clean.csv`) has 600 rows covering ages 0 to 99 across six years (2019–2024). Unlike the Structural Survey data, the GWS-STATPOP register covers the entire permanent resident population at the building and dwelling level, meaning that living space values are calculated from a full population count rather than a sample. There are no missing values in this dataset and no confidence intervals are published alongside the values. The column name `wohnfläche (in m2) pro person` contains special characters (the `ä` umlaut) that require consistent encoding handling during loading; the data acquisition script handles this by reading the CSV with the default UTF-8 encoding, which preserves the character correctly.

Generation labels are not stored in the processed files. In the Streamlit application, generations are derived dynamically by computing `birth_year = time_period - alter` and applying the project's generation definition table (defined in `app_config.py`). This avoids redundancy and keeps the processed files schema-stable as the project's generation boundaries evolve. The generation boundaries used are: Silent Generation (born ≤ 1945), Babyboomers (1946–1964), Generation X (1965–1980), Millennials / Gen Y (1981–1996), Generation Z (1997–2012).

The cantonal homeownership dataset (`wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026_clean.csv`) has 162 rows covering 27 cantons across six years. Confidence intervals are generally small — mostly below 2 percentage points — reflecting the large sample size of the Structural Survey at the cantonal level. No missing values are present. This dataset is retained for reference and potential future extensions but is not directly rendered in the current Streamlit visualisation.

One important methodological limitation applies across all occupancy and space indicators in this dimension: they reflect **household-level tenure status**, not individual ownership. A young adult still living in a parental owner-occupied home is recorded as residing in an owner-occupied household, which inflates the apparent ownership rate for younger generations such as Generation Z. Conversely, when multiple adults share the same dwelling, the m² per person figure is compressed, which reduces the apparent living space for Generation Z even in owner-occupied homes. These artefacts are inherent to the household-level measurement design of the Structural Survey and are explicitly noted in the visualisation narrative.

A second limitation specific to the oldest age group is the care home exclusion described in the data governance section. Because the Structural Survey only covers persons in private households, those who have moved into care homes or assisted living do not appear in the data. The remaining Silent Generation respondents in the dataset are therefore disproportionately those who continue to live in large owner-occupied homes — skewing both the occupancy rate and the living space figure for this generation upward relative to the true population average.

Overall, the data quality is sufficient for the intended visualisation goal: to show broad generational patterns in housing tenure and living space in Switzerland. The GWS-STATPOP living space data is particularly reliable due to its register-based coverage. The Structural Survey occupancy data is suitable for trend analysis and generational comparison, provided that the household-level measurement artefacts and the care home exclusion are communicated transparently to the user. The main limitations are the household-level tenure definition, the exclusion of collective households, the small-sample confidence intervals for extreme age groups, and the dynamic derivation of generation labels from age data rather than direct individual birth year records.

### Details Processed Datasets: Who Decides – SELECTS Survey Waves

The three processed datasets for the **"Who decides?"** dimension are `selects_2015_clean.csv`, `selects_2019_clean.csv` and `selects_2023_clean.csv`. They are stored in `data/whodecide/processed/` and are the direct inputs to the Streamlit visualisation. All three files share the same harmonised variable schema described in the raw data section (@tbl-whodecides-data-catalogue).

**Processing steps and rationale:**
The 2015 dataset originates from the raw Stata file `726_Selects2015_PES_Data_v1.03.dta`. It was converted to CSV format and the turnout variable was standardised: the source column `f11100r` (values 1.0/0.0) was mapped to the binary `f11100rec` column (1 = voted, 0 = did not vote) used consistently across all three waves. The 2019 and 2023 datasets were already available as processed CSVs with `f11100rec` present. For all three waves, column names are lowercased and stripped of whitespace at load time. The following derived variables are added by the preprocessing function `_prepare()` in `who_decides_section.py`:

- `generation`: assigned from `birthyear` using fixed cut-off points (Silent ≤ 1945, Boomers ≤ 1964, Gen X ≤ 1980, Millennials ≤ 1996, Gen Z > 1996). Respondents without a valid birth year receive the label `Unknown` and are excluded from all aggregations.
- `voted`: numeric conversion of `f11100rec`; only rows with a non-negative value are retained, which removes invalid survey codes.
- `political_interest`: numeric conversion of `f10100`; codes −99, −98 and 9 are set to `NaN`.
- `trust_avg`: row-wise mean of `f11301`, `f11302` and `f11305`; codes −99 and −98 are set to `NaN` per column before averaging.
- `demo_satisfaction`: binary recode of `f12010`; value 1 maps to 1 (satisfied), value 2 maps to 0 (not satisfied); codes −99, −98, 8 and 9 are set to `NaN`.
- `lr_scale`: left–right self-placement on a 1–5 scale. In 2015, derived from `f12900main7` (7-point scale) using the fixed mapping `{1:1.0, 2:1.5, 3:2.5, 4:3.0, 5:3.5, 6:4.5, 7:5.0}`; invalid codes (−99, −98, 8, 9) set to `NaN`. In 2019 and 2023, derived from `f12900rec` (values 10/20/30/40/50) by dividing by 10; invalid codes set to `NaN`.

The processed files do not contain a `survey_year` column. The year dimension is introduced at application load time by the `_load_frames()` function, which reads each file separately and stores the resulting DataFrames in a dictionary keyed by election year (2015, 2019, 2023).

**How to access and reproduce:**
The processed CSV files are read directly by `who_decides_section.py` via the paths `SELECTS_2015_PATH_CSV`, `SELECTS_2019_PATH` and `SELECTS_2023_PATH`. The `_load_frames()` function is decorated with `@st.cache_data`, so the files are loaded once per Streamlit session. To reproduce the preprocessing for the 2015 wave, the raw `.dta` file at `data/whodecide/raw/726_Selects2015_PES_Data_v1.03.dta` must be available. The 2019 and 2023 processed CSVs can be used directly without access to the original raw files.

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The processed files contain the following approximate row counts after filtering for valid turnout responses: SELECTS 2015 (N ≈ 5 337), SELECTS 2019 (N ≈ 6 664) and SELECTS 2023 (N ≈ 5 033). Missing value rates differ across variables: `lr_scale` has the highest missingness (respondents declining to self-place), while `political_interest` and `demo_satisfaction` have low missingness with slightly higher rates among younger respondents. The `trust_avg` variable is a constructed composite whose three components (`f11301`, `f11302`, `f11305`) may vary slightly in wording between waves — it should not be interpreted as a validated psychometric scale. All remaining quality characteristics and limitations are documented in the raw data section above.

### Details Processed Dataset: Who Owns – Occupancy Type by Age

The processed occupancy type dataset `bfs_bewohnertyp_20260414_clean.csv` is derived from the SE sheets of the raw file `data/whoOwns/raw/bfs_bewohnertyp_groesse.xlsx`. It is the primary data source for the ownership vs. renting chart in the Streamlit application. The dataset contains person counts and share percentages by single age year, occupancy type and reference year for Switzerland, covering the period 2019 to 2024.

**Processing steps and rationale:**
The raw Excel workbook contains one sheet per survey year for each data type, identified by the sheet name prefix `SE` (e.g. `SE2024`, `SE2023`). The data acquisition function `load_bfs_bewohnertyp_groesse_data` in `01_data_acquisition/load_sources.py` iterates over all matching sheets, reads each with header row index 2 (skipping the FSO title and subtitle rows above the column names), and drops all columns whose names start with `Unnamed` (artefacts of merged cells in the Excel layout). Since the reference year is encoded in the sheet name rather than in a data column, the year is extracted from the sheet name using a regular expression and added as the `time_period` column. Rows where the `Alter` (age) column is not numeric — which includes sub-total and label rows at the top and bottom of each sheet — are removed. All numeric columns are coerced to float, replacing non-numeric placeholders (e.g. dash characters used by the FSO to mark suppressed cells) with `NaN`. Column names are then standardised to lowercase with whitespace stripped via `standardize_columns`. The processed file is saved with `index=False` so no row index is written to the CSV.

**How to access and reproduce:**
The processed file is generated by running `01_data_acquisition/load_sources.py` from the project root. The script writes the output directly to `data/whoOwns/processed/bfs_bewohnertyp_20260414_clean.csv`. No additional configuration is required. The Streamlit application loads this file at startup via the `load_bewohnertyp_data` function in `04_deployment/who_owns_section.py`, which applies two further transformations at load time: it renames `Mieter oder Genossenschafter` to `Mieter / Genossenschaftler` for display consistency, and it renames `Andere Situation2)` to `Andere Situation` by stripping the footnote marker. It also filters the data to retain only the two occupancy types used in the charts (`Eigentümer` and `Mieter / Genossenschaftler`), discarding `Andere Situation` and `Total`.

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The file contains 2,040 rows — each combination of `alter`, `bewohnertyp` and `time_period` is unique with no duplicates. The `absolute zahlen` column has a small number of `NaN` values above age 90 where the FSO suppresses low-reliability estimates (flagged with `*` in `datenqualität`); these do not affect generation-level aggregations. The `anteil in %` column is internally consistent: category shares sum to approximately 100% per age and year, confirming no rows were lost during loading. All further quality characteristics are documented in the raw data section above.

### Details Processed Dataset: Who Owns – Living Space by Age

The processed living space dataset `bfs_wohnflaeche_20260414_clean.csv` is derived from the GWS-STATPOP sheets of the raw file `data/whoOwns/raw/bfs_bewohnertyp_groesse.xlsx`. It is the primary data source for the living space (m²/person) charts in the Streamlit application. The dataset contains average living space per person in square metres by single age year and reference year for Switzerland, covering the period 2019 to 2024.

**Processing steps and rationale:**
The data acquisition function `load_bfs_bewohnertyp_groesse_data` identifies GWS-STATPOP sheets by checking for the keyword `gws` in the sheet name (case-insensitive). The same loading logic as for the occupancy type sheets is applied: header row index 2, removal of unnamed columns, year inference from sheet name, numeric type coercion and column name standardisation. Because GWS-STATPOP data is register-based rather than survey-based, the sheets do not contain confidence interval columns or quality flags, resulting in a simpler schema than the occupancy type data. The output is saved to `data/whoOwns/processed/bfs_wohnflaeche_20260414_clean.csv`.

**How to access and reproduce:**
The processed file is generated by running `01_data_acquisition/load_sources.py`. The Streamlit application loads it via the `load_wohnflaeche_data` function in `04_deployment/who_owns_section.py`, which identifies the living space column dynamically by searching for `m2` in the column name (case-insensitive) and renames it to `sqm_per_person` for use in computations. Generation labels are again derived dynamically from age and year.

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The file contains 600 rows — exactly 100 age values (0–99) multiplied by 6 years (2019–2024) — with no missing values, consistent with the register-based coverage of GWS-STATPOP. Values range from approximately 27 m²/person (infants sharing a household) to approximately 80 m²/person (persons above age 85, reflecting the empty-nest effect and care home exclusion). Values are stable across years with a slow upward drift. No outliers were detected in the exploratory analysis.

### Details Processed Dataset: Who Owns – Cantonal Homeownership Rates

The processed cantonal homeownership dataset `wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026_clean.csv` is derived from the raw file `data/whoOwns/raw/wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026.csv` and enriched with canton name labels from `data/whoOwns/raw/metadaten_wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026.ods`. It provides homeownership rates by Swiss canton and year. This dataset is retained for reference and potential future visualisation extensions but is not directly rendered in the current Streamlit application.

**Processing steps and rationale:**
The raw CSV uses semicolons as delimiters, which is standard for BFS statistical exports. The `load_wohneigentums_data` function reads the file with `sep=";"` and loads it into a DataFrame. The geo metadata ODS file is loaded separately via `load_geo_metadata`, which reads the `GEO` sheet and extracts the `CODE`, `LABEL_DE`, `LABEL_FR`, `LABEL_EN` and `LABEL_IT` columns. The canton name labels are joined onto the cantonal data via a left merge on the `geo` column, matching the BFS geographic codes (e.g. `CH010`) between the two files. Column names are then standardised to lowercase via `standardize_columns`. The enriched file is saved to `data/whoOwns/processed/wohneigentumsquote_kanton_2026_clean.csv`.

**How to access and reproduce:**
The processed file is generated by running `01_data_acquisition/load_sources.py`. It can be read directly from the project directory with any standard CSV reader using the default comma delimiter.

#### Data Characteristics and Quality

The file contains 162 rows covering 27 Swiss cantons across 6 years (2019–2024) with no missing values. After the geo metadata join, additional label columns (`label_de`, `label_fr`, `label_en`, `label_it`) are present. The `obs_value` ranges from approximately 19% (Geneva) to approximately 60% (Appenzell Innerrhoden), consistent with published FSO statistics. Confidence intervals are generally below 2 percentage points and all rows carry `obs_status = A`, confirming FSO publication quality. The canton label join achieves a 100% match rate.
